## Phill Agnew — Mount Everest's first measurement was 29,000 but surveyors reported
 it as 29,002. Here's why. | Nudge Newsletter

_From: `[email]` · 2026-06-05T08:45:21+00:00_

********************
Specific Number Bias
********************

​Read online ( https://a7046da1.click.kit-mail3.com/e5ue23xe09i7hl37gwxc8h85e20k7ilh2n4z8/m2h7h5h3p5228lsm/aHR0cHM6Ly9udWRnZS5raXQuY29tL3Byb2ZpbGU= )​

I stumbled across this Reddit post a few weeks back.

Everest surveyors added two feet to their measurement to appear accurate.
Rather than listing the exact measurement of 29,000, the British Royal Geographical Society declared Mount Everest's elevation at 29,002.

Clearly, the surveyors thought that rounded numbers seem less believable.

Something that numerous studies have since proven.

-----------------------
Can You Spare 17 Cents?
-----------------------

In 1994, Santos, Leve and Pratkanis asked three female actors to approach 289 adults¹.

Each actor was instructed to ask the passersby for change. But there was a twist.

Half asked:

"Can you spare 17¢?"

The other half asked:

"Can you spare a quarter?"

The researchers wanted to know if asking for a specific number boosts donations.

Specific requests boosted donations by ~39%.
It worked; the specific number made people 39% more likely to donate than the general request. It also led to a higher donation total (despite the actors asking for less).

19 years later, 5 different researchers tested the effect again.

-------------------------
Can You Spare 37 Seconds?
-------------------------

The 1994 study proved specific numbers worked with money, but would it work with time?

In 2015, Guéguen and his colleagues headed to the streets of Brittany in France².

For this experiment, they recruited four female actors dressed identically all in black to ask passersby to complete a survey.

300 passersby were asked (150 men and 150 women).

However, 150 were asked:

"I wonder if you have a little time to spare to answer a survey."

The other 150 were asked

"I wonder if you have 37 seconds to spare to answer a survey."

Specific requests boosted compliance by 42.9%.
Of the 150 asked to spare a little time, only 63 agreed

Of the 150 asked to spare 37 seconds, 90 agreed.

A specific request boosted compliance by 42.9%.

Rounded numbers seem less believable. Specific numbers appear trustworthy.

So, when someone asks for 17 cents, we think, they must have a good reason.

When someone asks for 37 seconds, we think, this really won't take long.

And when Everest is measured at 29,002, we think that must be right!

The specific number bias is one of 85 principles you'll find in the Nudge Vaults. ## Most buyers see 87 touchpoints before your sales team enters the chat

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/61f5112e-d166-452b-9b67-4ba33ffea794/Sopro.png?t=1780520988)
Caption: 

### The news

Sopro’s [State of Prospecting 2026 report](https://sopro.io/resources/whitepapers/the-state-of-prospecting-26), drawing on 151 million outreach touchpoints, finds that the B2B buying journey is now overwhelmingly self-directed. 

At enterprise companies of 10,000+ employees, there are an average of 87 brand touchpoints before the first sales conversation even happens — meaning by the time a "lead" surfaces, buyers aren't exploring, they're confirming a choice they've mostly made. They estimate that more than 70% of the buyer’s journey has already happened before most people reach out to a brand. 

The report also found that 84% of buyers are more likely to engage with outreach if they already recognize the brand reaching out to them.

### What it means for marketers

* If you're not visible early, you may never make the shortlist. Lead gen is now about influence long before intent becomes visible.

* Brand familiarity has a major impact on getting a prospect to engage with outreach. Investing in brand pays off.

* Stop treating prospecting as a seasonal burst that switches on when pipeline dips. Buyers research continuously, so visibility has to compound year-round.

* Bad targeting now actively damages deliverability and sender reputation, so the value of AI is in helping you avoid sending the wrong messages.

““[B2B buyers are] using all the tools available to them and doing all the research themselves. They’re not speaking to sales as part of that information-gathering. It’s more about validation. By the time they come to you, they’ve usually built a shortlist and the winner tends to come from that shortlist.”“ — [Kit Smith, author of the 2026 State of Prospecting](https://www.thedrum.com/news/why-87-of-b2b-buying-happens-before-you-even-know-it)

## Is AI really stealing jobs from young people?

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/6bc87347-504e-48a4-8f6f-c36909e6a4f2/Atlantic.png?t=1780520999)
Caption: 

### The news

The unemployment rate for recent college grads has climbed to a decade-plus high, and plenty of headlines have pinned it on AI displacing entry-level white-collar work. But [The Atlantic's Rogé Karma argues](https://www.theatlantic.com/economy/2026/04/job-market-artificial-intelligence/686659/) that nearly every available data point suggests whatever is holding back young workers has little to do with AI. 

Economists found that young workers without college degrees have fared even worse than graduates since 2023 — the opposite of what you'd expect if AI were replacing white-collar roles, and enough to make one of them doubt this is an AI story at all. 

Researchers who tested five different measures of AI exposure against employment outcomes found no meaningful correlation. Meanwhile, sectors with more AI usage have seen slightly better outcomes, and a NY Fed survey found more firms hiring because of AI than cutting.

### What it means for marketers

* Be careful echoing the AI-disruption narrative in your content. The more likely culprit is a broad hiring slowdown driven by economic uncertainty, not automation.

* The labor market is genuinely hard to read right now, which should make all of us more skeptical of confident, sweeping AI predictions in our own thought leadership.

In the wake of creator films _Obsession_ and _Backrooms_—the latter of which just became A24’s first film to cross $100M at the box office—it seems [all of Hollywood](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/youtube-box-office-potential/) is in a mad dash to find the next Curry Barker or Kane Parsons. 

This week, we’ve heard firsthand rumblings from sources at major agencies, streamers, and studios that the time to make creator projects is _now_.

**We called up Drew Shenfield, a talent manager at Mosaic that reps both **[creators](https://www.tiktok.com/@deadeyebrakeman?lang=en)** and traditional talent, to hear why → **

“I think Hollywood is a reactive place, and a lot of the time they don't get the right message from stuff,” Shenfield told us. 

**What studios need to do differently: **For Shenfield, the most important note for Hollywood isn’t just greenlighting more creator horror movies, but working with creators across all genres that have direct lines with a younger audience. After all, over half of all _Obsession_ viewers were [under 25](https://variety.com/2026/film/box-office/backrooms-box-office-record-opening-weekend-obsession-jumps-star-wars-crumbles-1236763355/). 

“It's very hard for somebody who's been in the business for 40 years to get a young cast to feel authentic,” Shenfield said. ”What [_Backrooms_ and _Obsession_] did so well was resonate with an audience that is starving for it.” 

**Why is this moment happening now?** Shenfield theorizes that constricting opportunities in traditional film and television have led to an abundance of creators, which has given way to lots of original IP across platforms.

“Maybe back in the day, those [creators] would be writing on _Key and Peele_ or staffed in a room, but because that opportunity is so tough, now they have to go self-start,” Shenfield said.

**How we see it:** As Syd told Warner Bailey on _[AvA LIVE](https://www.youtube.com/live/oXysx-U2_i8?si=SmOlsE0A65sbL43S&t=2864)_ earlier this week, the core of this movement isn’t about the format—it’s about the creator. Original stories from creators with strong visions will win over repetitive formats in the long run.

"Backrooms feels like something that everybody on the internet had a hand in creating. So when that comes out in theaters, [viewers say] 'I want a thing that I had a hand in,'" Samir said yesterday [on TBPN](https://x.com/tbpn/status/2062538305561067602?s=20).
